title: Service Communication and Cascading Failure
html:
Chapter 3 established why a payment timeout cannot be treated as a definite failure. There is a related problem during the request itself. When Checkout Service waits for another service, its handler, memory, and outbound connection may still be occupied. If enough calls are delayed, new customers begin waiting even when the application has spare CPU.

You can see the same mechanism in traffic approaching a blocked road. Cars accumulate well before the obstruction, although the road in front of each driver is clear. In a cascading failure, requests accumulate in callers that are waiting on a slower downstream service.

Baodium encountered this after adding an external fraud-scoring provider to checkout. Fraud Service prepared the assessment and asked the provider to approve, deny, or request manual review. The initial calls completed promptly, but several weeks later provider latency increased substantially. Checkout requests accumulated, and Order Service ran out of available workers while its CPU utilization was low. The provider was returning valid decisions. We need to understand why the waiting callers were exhausting Checkout Service.

Cross-Service Failure Propagation

Let’s consider one checkout during the incident. Order Service assigned a worker to the request, validated the cart, and called Fraud Service. Fraud Service took a slot in its provider client and sent the assessment. The Order Service worker then waited for Fraud Service, while Fraud Service waited for the provider. Figure Figure shows how these waits are nested.

Order Service used blocking workers, the model most web frameworks use by default, in which each request occupies one worker thread from start to finish. A worker waiting for network I/O used very little CPU, but it could not process another checkout, so as provider calls took longer, more incoming checkouts found every worker already busy with an earlier request. Fraud Service had its own limit on active provider requests, and once those slots were all in use, new assessments queued inside Fraud Service before they reached the provider. Their callers in Order Service waited through that queue as well. It is the pattern from Chapter 1 again, a queue deep in the request path using up workers much closer to the customer, and it is the motorway jam in software form.

Little’s Law from Chapter 2 confirmed the diagnosis. One Order Service instance received 200 checkouts per second, and each of them spent at least 2.05 seconds in the part of the request that depended on fraud evaluation, including the processing around the provider call. Sustaining that rate would have required 200×2.05=410200 \times 2.05 = 410200×2.05=410 workers for that interval alone, against a configured pool of 300. Requests queued or failed instead of completing at the rate they arrived.

An asynchronous runtime would not have avoided this. A coroutine releases its thread while it waits, but the request still uses memory and may still occupy a connection or an admission slot, so the same investigation would run against those resources instead.

Measuring Dependency Slowdown

With the worker pool full, the first proposal was to add workers. It is the change most engineers reach for, and the useful first step is to find out what the existing workers are doing. At Baodium, they were waiting on Fraud Service, and Fraud Service already limited how many calls it sent to the provider. More Order Service workers would not have sent the provider a single extra request. They would only have admitted more checkouts into the wait, each with its own worker and memory. The queue would have become deeper and spread further back toward the customer, like opening more lanes onto a motorway that is blocked ahead.

A trace of a delayed checkout showed that most of its time went to the Fraud Service call. Inside Fraud Service, separate timers showed how long each request waited to get a provider client slot and how long it waited after the request was sent. The order in which these two values changed told the team where to look. If acquisition time rises while provider-call duration is unchanged, the cause is local, such as contention in the client, additional callers, or more requests. If provider-call duration rises first and acquisition time rises after it, longer calls are occupying the client slots. Fraud Service’s timers showed the second pattern.

That left the design decision the team had never made. What should checkout do once waiting for a fraud decision starts to interfere with everything else it has to do?

Required Results and Deferred Work

A confirmed purchase required an acceptable fraud decision, a payment authorization, an inventory reservation, and a committed order record. The original handler also waited for Notification Service to send the confirmation email. These calls did not all deserve the same treatment, and the difference lies in the meaning of each call for the correctness of the purchase.

Without an acceptable fraud decision and an authorization, checkout could not confirm the purchase. A confirmation email is different. Once the order is committed, the purchase exists whether or not the email goes out. If email delivery failed and checkout returned a generic error at that point, the customer might well try to buy the same items again. The handler needed to return the confirmed order and send the notification separately.

Fraud evaluation could not be treated that way, because payment could not begin without an acceptable decision. If the fraud response was missing, checkout had to return a pending or unavailable result, according to its policy.

So before you choose a timeout or add a queue, decide what each dependency must deliver and what the caller does when it cannot. This one question, asked for every dependency, prevents more cascading failures than any setting. Table Table shows those decisions for checkout.

The result required from each checkout dependency.
Dependency Required result Incomplete outcome
Fraud Acceptable decision before payment. Defer assessment without starting payment.
Payment Confirmed authorization before proceeding. Reconcile an uncertain authorization.
Inventory Confirmed reservation before order confirmation. Resolve uncertainty or compensate a definitive rejection.
Notification Delivery after order confirmation. Retry delivery from durable work.

Baodium took notification off the request path by writing an OrderConfirmed event to the transactional outbox from Chapter 3 in the same transaction as the order. A notification outage could then delay emails without slowing the checkout request.

The same table tells you which calls can run concurrently. Independent reads, such as the product-page lookups from Chapter 1, can be issued together. Starting payment while fraud evaluation is still unresolved would break the checkout policy, even if it made the response faster. When you do run calls in parallel, you also need a rule for how they complete. The caller may need both results, it may be able to return a partial result, or it may need to cancel the unfinished call once the other one fails. That rule belongs in the operation’s contract.

Outbound Concurrency Admission

Once a slow fraud result could lead to a deferred assessment instead of a failed checkout, Order Service could limit how many requests waited for fraud evaluation at any one time. Each instance was given 80 concurrent outbound fraud calls. A handler tried to acquire a permit1 before sending the call, and if all 80 permits were in use, it recorded a pending assessment and returned the checkout reference without calling Fraud Service at all. As with the semaphore in Chapter 1’s bounded lookup, acquiring a permit checks and reserves capacity in one atomic step, so two handlers cannot both take the last permit.

A limit like this, reserved for calls to one dependency, is called a bulkhead, after the walls that divide a ship’s hull into watertight compartments. If one compartment floods, the walls stop the water from reaching the rest, and the ship does not sink. In software, the bulkhead stops calls to one slow dependency from occupying every worker the caller has, so the rest of the service continues to work.

Why does Order Service need its own limit when Fraud Service already has one? Suppose Fraud Service accepts network connections but stops processing requests. Its internal limit protects Fraud Service, while the Order Service handlers waiting to reach it pile up on the other side. Only a limit on Order Service’s side, applied before the outbound call, protects Order Service’s workers. As a general rule, each service needs its own limit on calls to a dependency rather than relying on the dependency’s limits.

Fraud Service, in turn, limits the evaluations it accepts from all callers. In this configuration, it admitted at most 80 evaluations per instance. Each evaluation retained its permit through all of its provider attempts and retry delays, and the provider client did not add a second request queue behind that limit.

Queueing and Rejection

A queue in front of the limit can help when a short burst will clear before the waiting requests lose their value. If you add one, give it a maximum size and a maximum waiting time, and make both consistent with the caller’s deadline, using the queue-sizing rule from Chapter 2.

For the fraud path, the checkout team chose to either admit each request without waiting or defer it. Waiting in another local queue would spend the customer’s deadline without producing a risk decision, and durable deferred processing was already available for work that could not start promptly.

This choice changes what the customer receives. Some checkouts that used to wait until they timed out now receive a pending result sooner, and the application has to complete or expire those assessments according to its recovery policy. Recording a pending result also has a cost, because it uses a handler and a database write. The fraud bulkhead limits outbound waiting, but the rate at which Order Service can accept checkouts is still limited by its own ingress admission and by its database capacity.

Outbound Concurrency Allocation

The 80-permit allocation came from two numbers specific to Baodium, the provider’s allowance and the checkout deadline, so another service with a different provider or deadline would need its own figure. To find it, the team ran checkout at its normal traffic and raised the number of permitted evaluations until the slowest ones began to miss the response budget. The highest setting that still met the budget became the local concurrency limit.

The provider imposed both request-rate and concurrent-call limits. They are different constraints, because a slow response increases the number of simultaneous calls even when the arrival rate is unchanged. The final allocation therefore depended on provider measurements as well as local load tests.

Per-instance limits also add up. Additional replicas, the extra instances during a deployment, other applications that use the same provider account, and background recovery workers all contribute to the provider’s total demand, just as you saw with database sessions in Chapter 2.

Chapter 9 develops how such limits are calibrated across a fleet.

Decision review

Where does the extra second come from?

Checkout gives fraud evaluation a one-second budget, and Order Service admits at most 80 concurrent fraud calls per instance. The provider has slowed. Evaluations that used to return in about 80 ms now take about two seconds, so nearly every call runs out of budget and the handler gives up. Your on-call engineer proposes raising the fraud deadline to three seconds so that evaluations can complete.

Raise the deadline to three seconds. The provider is slow, not broken, and the results are still arriving.

Retain the one-second deadline and defer the evaluation, returning a pending checkout.

Retain the deadline and raise the admission limit from 80 to 240, so that more evaluations can run at once.

A lets the two-second evaluations finish, but look at what it does to throughput. If each call occupies a permit for two seconds, 80 permits support about 80/2=4080 / 2 = 4080/2=40 completions per second per instance, against 200 checkouts arriving. The three-second timeout is a cap, not the mean, and if calls slow further and use the full three seconds, the figure falls to about 27 per second. Compare both numbers with the arrival rate and the full checkout deadline before changing the cap.

C allows more calls to wait but gives you no evidence that the provider can complete more evaluations. At the same arrival rate, it may raise concurrency without improving throughput, and it lets more caller memory and more workers be occupied.

B preserves the one-second response time and records the unfinished evaluation as durable work, and the customer receives a pending checkout reference. Recovery then needs its own admission limit, a status endpoint, and a rule that prevents payment before an acceptable fraud decision. A local timeout must not cause recovery to duplicate remote work that is still running.

B preserves the checkout response contract. A can be reasonable if the product accepts a slower checkout and tests show enough completion capacity, so the choice depends on those two requirements.

End-to-End Request Deadlines

Admission controls how many checkouts wait for fraud evaluation. The next decision is how long each admitted checkout may wait.

Think of a road trip on which you must arrive by six in the evening. Every leg of the journey, every stop for fuel, and every traffic delay has to fit into the time that is left. You cannot give each leg a fresh day of its own. A request deadline works the same way. Baodium chose a maximum of one second for the complete Fraud Service call, checked against the rest of checkout, and that second had to cover transit, local processing, every provider attempt, any retry delays, and the return trip. The provider itself receives less than the full second (Figure Figure).

To choose an allowance like this, start from the customer’s response requirement and look at representative checkout traces. Payment, inventory, local commits, and building the response all still need time after the fraud decision arrives. Then test the proposed split with slow dependencies and realistic variation, and measure end-to-end checkout duration, because the 99th percentiles of individual steps cannot be added to give the 99th percentile of the whole request.

The caller should also check how much time is left just before it starts fraud evaluation. If earlier steps have already used most of the request’s budget, it can shorten the fraud allowance or defer the assessment without sending the call.

Deadlines and Attempt Timeouts

A deadline applies to the whole operation, while an attempt timeout applies to a single call made during that operation. If a caller makes three attempts and gives each one a fresh one-second timeout, the request may already have exceeded its total deadline before cleanup and response handling begin.

Suppose an assessment has one second available, and the first provider attempt uses half of it. Any retry delay and the next attempt have to fit into the half second that is left, with some time left for recording and returning the result. Waiting for a connection or stream obeys the same rule, because that wait uses up the operation’s budget before the request is even sent.

Check what your client’s timeout settings measure, because the names are often misleading. A read timeout usually limits a single read or a gap with no data, not the whole response. In Python’s requests library, for example, the read timeout limits the time between bytes from the server, so a server that sends a byte every few seconds can extend a call far beyond what the timeout suggests. Domain Name System (DNS) resolution, connection setup, and Transport Layer Security (TLS) negotiation may also have their own settings. The integration needs one overall limit that covers the entire local attempt.

You can test this without waiting for a production outage. A stub, or a fault-injection proxy such as Toxiproxy, can delay connection setup, delay the response headers, or send the response body slowly. Each case should finish within the intended overall deadline, plus the cleanup time you have measured.

Deadlines Between Services

Order Service passes the unused part of the fraud budget to Fraud Service, which uses it when it starts provider work. Each hop subtracts the time that has already passed instead of starting again with its own default allowance. This is called deadline propagation, and its value increases as call chains get longer.

The format used to pass the deadline needs care as well. A monotonic clock reading is fine for measuring elapsed time inside one process. Another host cannot interpret it, though, and absolute timestamps depend on the two hosts’ clocks matching. gRPC avoids this by sending the time left as a duration, which the receiving service turns into a local deadline when the request arrives. If your transport has no built-in deadline, agree on a similar representation and decide how each service accounts for clock differences.

To check that propagation works, delay a request inside Fraud Service before provider work begins. The provider attempt should then receive less time. If it receives the original allowance, the downstream call can finish after the caller’s deadline has expired.

Cancellation and Continuing Work

When a caller times out, the work it started can carry on without it. Think of ordering a meal and then leaving the restaurant because it is taking too long. Unless someone tells the kitchen, the cook goes on cooking, using the stove and ingredients for an order that has already been cancelled. Remote work is similar. It may go on using a connection or a provider slot after the caller has given up, so cancellation and resource cleanup need their own mechanisms and their own measurements.

Let’s consider a handler that starts a provider call in a background task and waits for it with a timeout. When the wait expires, the handler returns, but the task is still running and still occupies its HTTP client slot. In Python, for example, calling result(timeout=1) on a future from a thread pool returns control after one second, while the thread carries on with the call. If the handler releases its admission permit as soon as it returns, another request can start alongside the still-running task, and after enough timeouts, the number of active client calls can rise well past the configured admission limit.

Baodium tied each permit to the work it covered. A permit was released only when that work finished or when local cancellation had completed. If a library returns earlier than that, you need separate accounting for the tasks still using resources.

Cancellation also has to reach retry delays and nested calls. A handler that is sleeping before another attempt should stop when its request is canceled, unless it has handed the work over to durable recovery on purpose.

The remote side needs its own check. Closing the local connection does not tell you that the provider stopped processing the request, and the client can release its socket while the provider finishes the assessment. For payment and inventory writes, the operation identity and reconciliation rules from Chapter 3 still apply. For capacity, it means that attempts which ended locally may still be using provider capacity, so your rate and retry limits have to allow for them. A cancellation test should check that local resources are released and, where the provider exposes the information, whether remote work continued.

Retry Eligibility and Ownership

Retries at several layers multiply. If the API gateway, the service mesh, and the client library each make up to three attempts, one checkout can become twenty-seven provider calls. The way to prevent that is to give retries to a single layer. Baodium gave provider retries to Fraud Service, because it had the assessment identity, the provider contract, and the deadline, and retries for that route were turned off in the API gateway, the service mesh, and the provider’s software development kit (SDK). Check those layers in your own system before you add retries anywhere, because some service meshes and SDKs retry certain failures by default, and those retries ignore your deadline and cannot check whether the operation is safe to repeat.

Before you write any retry code, separate the outcomes the handler can see, because they need different responses and only some of them are safe to retry. A connection failure that is known to have happened before the request was sent may allow another attempt. A completed approval, denial, or manual-review decision ends the assessment. A timeout after the request was sent may call for a lookup or a repeat under the provider’s idempotency contract, because the earlier request could still be running, as Chapter 3 described.

The timeout value also decides whether retrying is useful at all. If provider calls consistently take two seconds, repeated half-second attempts will almost never get a decision, and if abandoned requests are still running at the provider, each retry adds to the provider’s load.

For eligible transient failures, Fraud Service waited a bounded, randomized delay before retrying. The randomness, called jitter, spreads retries out so that many failing requests do not retry at the same moment, a common source of synchronized bursts. Fraud Service checked the time left before waiting and again before sending, and it applied both a maximum number of attempts per assessment and an overall retry allowance across all assessments. Once that allowance was used up during an outage, further assessments were deferred instead of retried.

The provider was taking about two seconds to respond, longer than checkout’s one-second allowance. A circuit breaker could stop new synchronous calls after recent timeouts and slow responses, while a few later probes tested recovery. A breaker that watched only HTTP error codes would miss this incident because the provider returned valid decisions, just too late. The admission limit was still necessary to protect the provider while the breaker gathered evidence. Chapter 9 develops the thresholds and recovery settings.

Integrating an External Decision Service

The checkout handler had three distinct responsibilities. It created or retrieved the durable risk assessment, admitted the outbound call within its deadline, and recorded the provider’s decision against the assessment’s current input version. Separating those steps in the implementation made each failure path easier to test. The repository methods below are illustrative.

The unique database constraint makes concurrent requests reuse the same assessment, and a saved result can be returned without another provider call. Before dispatching an unresolved assessment, checkout allocates a child deadline from the request’s unused time and attempts to acquire a permit.

A missing permit sends the assessment into deferred recovery. After an admitted provider call, the result can be recorded only against the same input revision that was evaluated.

Provider timeouts or unavailable results enter the unresolved-assessment procedure described earlier in the chapter. A completed evaluation uses a guarded database transition.

Two handlers for the same checkout can also run at the same time. A unique constraint prevents them from creating two assessments, because an application-level read and a separate insert would let both handlers find that no assessment exists yet. When the insert conflicts, the second handler retrieves the assessment the first one created.

If the insert returns no row, the handler selects the existing assessment by checkout ID and input version and continues with that one, so both submissions refer to the same assessment and the provider receives one evaluation request. The constraint includes the input version as well as the checkout, so that a changed cart can still get a new, linked assessment later. You could instead lock the checkout row for the whole handler, but as Chapter 3 explained, a lock that is still in place during a slow provider call occupies a database connection for the entire call.

The deferred update is conditional. If another handler has already recorded an approval, a late timeout must not replace it with a pending state, so the method returns the recorded outcome when the assessment has already been resolved. The decision update also checks that the assessment still applies to the current checkout inputs, so a canceled checkout or a changed cart cannot proceed to payment because of an earlier approval.

The outbound client has no retry policy of its own. Fraud Service owns provider retries and receives the inherited deadline, and the client checks the time left before sending and finishes its local cleanup before the permit is released. If caller cancellation interrupts the handler before it records a deferred result, the assessment is not lost, because background recovery can still find the unfinished record created before the call.

Pending-Operation API Contracts

A ride-hailing app may show “finding a driver” while dispatch continues. Checkout needed the same kind of clear status, telling the customer that fraud verification was pending, that no payment had been taken, and that the result could be checked later.

For a deferred fraud evaluation, Baodium returned the checkout reference with a message explaining that verification was in progress and that no payment had been taken. In HTTP terms, this is the asynchronous pattern of returning 202 Accepted and a uniform resource locator (URL) for checking status.2 Some APIs also include a Retry-After header suggesting how soon the client should check again, which stops polling from turning into a load problem of its own.

The status endpoint read the stored checkout state and never submitted another evaluation, so customers refreshing the page added inexpensive status reads but no provider calls. Recovery workers submitted the deferred evaluations under their own rate and concurrency allocation, which they shared with live requests so that a backlog could not use up all of the provider access. Each recovery attempt received a new execution deadline but reused the original assessment identity.

The application also distinguished a missing provider decision from a completed decision that required human review, because the two need different handling (Table Table).

Unfinished evaluation and manual review require different recovery work.
State Next step
RISK_EVALUATION_PENDING A worker obtains or recovers the provider decision.
RISK_MANUAL_REVIEW The risk-review process supplies the required judgment.

A delayed approval needed revalidation before payment. By the time it arrived, the price, the cart, delivery eligibility, or risk-relevant account data could have changed. Different inputs required a new assessment linked to the old one, and a price change could require the customer to confirm the purchase again.

Baodium also decided how long a deferred checkout could be continued and what would happen when that period expired. If recovery could no longer clear the backlog within that policy, accepting more deferred checkouts would mean making promises the application could not honor. Asynchronous completion needs status retrieval, expiry, cancellation, and revalidation, in addition to the worker that eventually calls the provider.

Dependency Slowdown and Recovery Testing

The team tested the revised path with a provider stub that could return decisions, reject requests, delay responses, or never respond, so they could check the application under specific conditions instead of waiting for the production provider to misbehave.

When the stub returned valid decisions slowly, the test checked the number of active fraud calls, the deferred outcomes, and whether unrelated requests still completed normally, which is the decisive test of a bulkhead. The load generator recorded the arrival rate it achieved, so that its own waiting could not reduce the intended load, as Chapter 1 described. When the stub never responded, the test checked deadlines and local cleanup, because active client requests and background tasks must not accumulate after their callers have returned.

To verify retry ownership, the team recorded every attempt the stub received. Measuring at the provider boundary caught extra attempts added by infrastructure or SDK settings, which a counter inside the application’s retry loop would have missed.

Recovery was tested with a backlog of pending assessments while live checkouts continued. Workers had to clear the backlog within the shared provider allocation, and canceled or expired checkouts had to stop before payment.

The release review needed business outcomes as well as technical ones, because lower checkout latency could mean only that more customers were receiving a pending result. The confirmed checkout rate, the time taken to complete deferred checkouts, and the number of expired checkouts showed whether those customers eventually got a useful result.

After release, each service reported measurements for its own part of the fraud check. Order Service reported assigned workers, active outbound fraud calls, and admission rejections. Fraud Service reported admitted evaluations, provider attempts, and the reason for each deferral, and separate timers for acquiring a client slot and for the provider call showed whether requests were waiting for local resources or for the provider. With those measurements and the recovery backlog metrics from Chapter 3, the on-call engineer could tell a slow live request apart from a deferred assessment and from a case waiting for human review, and each of these needs a different response. Chapter 8 develops this kind of measurement in depth.

Authentication and Authorization Boundaries

A Baodium merchant employee could open the order history and review purchases. The refund button appeared only for employees with a refund role. Hiding the button made the interface easier to use, but an employee could still send a refund request directly to the API. The server had to decide whether that request was permitted.

Authentication establishes who made the request. Authorization decides whether that principal may perform an action on a particular resource. Authority, as we used it in Chapter 3, identifies the service or record responsible for the final business outcome. These three decisions arise at different points in the request path.

An employee signs in and receives an application session. The gateway validates the session or an access token and can reject an unauthenticated request before it reaches Payment Service. An authenticated employee may still lack permission to refund order 4471. Payment Service uses the payment’s recorded merchant and the employee’s current membership and permissions to evaluate that operation. A merchant identifier supplied in the URL cannot establish ownership.

principal = request.authenticated_principal
payment = payments.get(request.payment_id)
if payment is None:
    raise NotFound()
if not memberships.active(principal.id, payment.merchant_id):
    raise NotFound()
if not permissions.allows(principal.id, "refund", payment):
    raise Forbidden()
refunds.request_once(payment, request.amount,
                     request.idempotency_key)

Here memberships and permissions query authoritative application data. The amount and refundable balance also require business validation inside the guarded operation. The example leaves that transaction to Chapter 3. Returning 404 when the employee cannot access the merchant avoids revealing whether another merchant’s payment exists. An employee who can see the payment but lacks the refund permission receives 403. An unauthenticated request receives 401 under the API’s authentication contract.

For browser applications, OpenID Connect can authenticate the user, while OAuth 2.0 provides a framework for delegated authorization. An application may use a server-managed session or validate access tokens at its APIs.3 These protocols establish useful credentials. The merchant-to-order relationship and refund policy still come from the application.

Internal calls require another distinction. Order Service may call Payment Service on behalf of the employee, but authenticating Order Service does not prove that the employee was entitled to request a refund. Payment Service needs trustworthy caller context and a contract for any delegated user authority. That may be a token issued for the receiving service or a server-side operation record whose approval the receiver can verify. Forwarding an unsigned user ID header would let a compromised caller choose another identity. An internal network address is no substitute for a service credential.

Role-based access control (RBAC) can establish that an employee has the refund capability. Attribute-based access control (ABAC) can further consider merchant membership, refund amount, regional policy, or the state of the payment. Production applications often combine both. A single merchant role would be inadequate for an employee with access to several merchants or a refund ceiling below the requested amount.

Authorization for Deferred Refunds

Now consider a refund that is approved at 10:00 but cannot reach the payment provider until 10:07. At 10:04, the merchant administrator revokes the employee’s refund permission. Should the worker proceed? The business contract must establish when authorization takes effect. For some operations, a durable approval at acceptance is sufficient. Others require the permission to be checked again just before dispatch. An organization may also require two people to approve an unusually large refund. The choice changes the stored record and the worker’s behavior.

A durable approval can refer to the principal, payment, amount, operation ID, policy revision, time of approval, and any expiry. The worker compares that approval with the queued operation before it contacts the provider. If the policy requires live permission checks, the worker performs them as well. A revoked or expired approval enters an auditable rejection or review state without issuing the external refund. The queue message itself grants no new permission.

def dispatch(refund):
    approval = approvals.get(refund.approval_id)
    if not approval.valid_for(refund):
        return refunds.send_for_review(refund.id)
    if not policy.permits_execution(approval, refund):
        return refunds.send_for_review(refund.id)
    provider.submit(refund, idempotency_key=refund.operation_id)

This snippet assumes the worker has already authenticated its own service identity and loaded the durable refund operation, and permits_execution applies the selected revocation policy, including a live permission check when execution requires one. If a permission revocation must stop an action that is concurrently being dispatched, a last-moment read alone cannot guarantee that outcome. The application needs a coordinated authorization boundary or a business rule that defines when dispatch becomes irrevocable. The payment result and reconciliation procedure are those of Chapter 3.

Other systems face this decision whenever a booking is confirmed later, a cloud resource is provisioned from a queue, or a deployment controller acts on an approval created earlier. Chapter 11 examines which service performs the resource check. Appendix C provides the corresponding security review and negative tests.

Required Commits and Deferred Notifications

Contract decisions like these come up well outside checkout. Let’s consider a booking service that reserves a seat, authorizes a payment, sends a receipt, and updates analytics. The traveler needs a confirmed reservation, while the receipt and analytics can arrive later, so the response waits only for committed reservation state and the payment result, and the receipt goes through a durable job.

Suppose the reservation takes 90 milliseconds, the payment authorization 180, and local processing 20, about 290 milliseconds in sequence before network and queueing delays. Running the reservation and payment concurrently would shorten that, but the two operations depend on each other. A payment authorized for a seat that turned out to be unavailable becomes compensation work, so the time saved is paid for in recovery complexity. If the payment provider cannot finish within the deadline, the API returns a durable pending booking with a retrievable operation ID, the same pattern as Baodium’s deferred fraud check. A small booking API, one transactional store, one bounded payment client, and a job path for receipts is a complete first design. More services are justified only when ownership or isolation requirements demand them.

Summary

The fraud provider never returned an error, and that is the lesson to carry with you. A dependency can damage your service by taking longer, because every extra second is a worker, a connection, and some memory that cannot serve anyone else. Errors are easy to notice. Slowness spreads until the queue reaches your own customers.

The team’s response is a sequence you can reuse. First decide what a request truly needs before it can succeed, and what can finish later. Then protect your own resources with a limit on outbound calls, give the whole request one deadline that every hop respects, let a single layer own retries, and turn work that cannot finish in time into a durable pending record the customer can check on. None of these controls makes the provider faster. They decide who waits, for how long, and what the customer is told.

Some dependency calls are expensive for a simpler reason. The caller asks for the same data again and again. Chapter 5 looks at storing a copy of that data, and at the freshness rules that make a copy safe to use.

Hidden assumptions

Assumption and scope & Checkout may defer fraud evaluation without beginning payment, provided the customer receives a durable reference and the assessment is completed or expired under a defined policy.
Condition that tests it & A dependency slows while callers continue admitting requests or retries.
Constraint or invariant & Order Service limits outbound fraud calls before sending. Fraud Service separately limits evaluations and provider requests. Live processing and recovery share the provider allocation.
Evidence and uncertainty & Provider-call duration rose from about 80 milliseconds to nearly two seconds. Client-acquisition delay rose after it, and Order Service ran out of available workers. Verification measures both bounded waiting and eventual checkout outcomes.

Still unknown: whether provider work continues after local cancellation, and whether deferred assessments can be completed under the recovery policy during an extended slowdown.
Signal and evaluation window & During the slowdown test, measure queue duration, occupied workers, and downstream attempts against the shared deadline.
Control and decision & Bound synchronous waiting and record unfinished assessments. Proceed to payment only after an acceptable risk decision, with current checkout data and a permitted state transition.
Owner and review trigger & The checkout owner defines customer outcomes and expiry. The Fraud Service owner manages provider admission, retry eligibility, and assessment recovery. Review after the test condition occurs or before expanding exposure.

  1. A permit is one unit of a concurrency limiter. Acquiring a permit increases the number of admitted calls by one, and releasing it reduces that number by one.↩︎
